column1: What does a Database Transaction Unit (DTU) measure in Azure SQL Database?
column2:
A blend of CPU, memory, and read/write I/O resources.
DTUs bundle resources rather than exposing separate CPU and memory choices.
Review source

column1: Why does the vCore model help with capacity planning for an on-premises SQL Server migration?
column2:
It exposes CPU and memory capacity more directly.
The selected hardware and compute size determine the available memory.
Review source

column1: Which vCore service tier provides budget-oriented compute and storage for moderate I/O latency requirements?
column2:
General Purpose.
Compute is separate from remote Azure Blob files, which replacement compute can reattach after a failure.
Review source

column1: What storage architecture gives Business Critical low I/O latency?
column2:
Locally attached SSD storage on the compute nodes.
Storage I/O latency is not a guarantee of end-to-end transaction response time.
Review source

column1: Which Business Critical feature offloads reporting queries from the primary replica?
column2:
Read scale-out to an included read-only secondary.
It uses separate compute capacity for read-only work.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL Database service tier supports a single database up to 128 TB?
column2:
Hyperscale.
General Purpose and Business Critical top out at 4 TB, subject to compute-size limits.
Review source

column1: Which components separate data storage from compute in the Hyperscale architecture?
column2:
Page servers.
The separate storage architecture lets compute scale without copying the entire database.
Review source

column1: What storage amount determines Hyperscale data storage charges?
column2:
Allocated data storage, rather than the maximum supported database size.
Allocated space is not necessarily the same as space occupied by rows.
Review source

column1: Which Hyperscale replica type supports independently sized read-only workloads?
column2:
A named replica.
Its compute can scale independently of the primary replica.
Review source

column1: How is provisioned compute billed when an Azure SQL Database is idle?
column2:
The provisioned compute capacity remains billable at its hourly rate.
Low activity does not automatically remove provisioned compute charges.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL Database compute tier automatically scales compute for intermittent demand?
column2:
Serverless.
It scales within the configured compute range.
Review source

column1: How is active serverless compute billed in Azure SQL Database?
column2:
Per second, based on CPU and memory usage, subject to configured minimums.
Billing is not based solely on CPU activity.
Review source

column1: Which charges continue while an Azure SQL Database serverless database is paused?
column2:
Storage charges.
Compute charges are zero during the paused period.
Review source

column1: What serverless performance tradeoff matters when a workload cannot tolerate delays after inactivity?
column2:
Compute warm-up or resume delays.
Provisioned compute avoids the serverless pause-and-resume tradeoff.
Review source

column1: What does the max degree of parallelism (MAXDOP) setting control?
column2:
The degree of intra-query parallelism.
It is not a hard cap on the total worker threads used by an entire query.
Review source

column1: Why does Microsoft recommend avoiding MAXDOP 0 in Azure SQL Database?
column2:
Excess parallelism can starve concurrent queries of CPU and worker resources.
Test MAXDOP changes under realistic concurrent loads, not only isolated queries.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL automatic tuning option corrects an execution plan regression?
column2:
FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN.
Azure defaults enable it, but inherited configuration or overrides can change its effective state.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL automatic tuning option creates indexes and checks their performance benefit?
column2:
CREATE_INDEX.
Azure defaults leave this option disabled.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL automatic tuning option removes eligible unused or duplicate indexes?
column2:
DROP_INDEX.
It is off under Azure defaults, protects unique indexes, and removes only duplicates in Business Critical.
Review source

column1: What happens when an automatically applied tuning change fails performance validation?
column2:
The service reverts the change.
Automatic tuning checks for a positive workload benefit after applying the recommendation.
Review source

column1: What validation is missing when you manually run a tuning recommendation's T-SQL script?
column2:
The automatic performance validation and reversal workflow.
Manual execution requires you to assess and reverse an unhelpful change.
Review source

column1: What happens to an existing Azure SQL database's compatibility level when Microsoft introduces a newer default?
column2:
It keeps its existing level until someone changes it.
An engine update does not automatically opt the database into new optimizer behavior.
Review source

column1: Which feature captures a query performance baseline before a compatibility-level upgrade?
column2:
Query Store.
Compare test results with the baseline and force a previous good plan to mitigate regressions.
Review source

column1: Which database-scoped configuration reduces cache memory consumed by single-use ad hoc plans?
column2:
OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADS.
It targets plan cache memory pressure rather than guaranteeing faster query execution.
Review source

column1: With ad hoc optimization enabled, what is cached after an ad hoc batch's first compilation?
column2:
A small compiled plan stub instead of the full compiled plan.
A repeat execution with the stub cached recompiles the batch and caches its full plan.
Review source

column1: Which database engine feature speeds recovery and rollback involving long-running transactions?
column2:
Accelerated database recovery (ADR).
It uses persisted row versions to avoid traditional lengthy undo of versioned changes.
Review source

column1: What is the enablement state of accelerated database recovery in Azure SQL Database?
column2:
Always enabled.
Customers cannot disable ADR for an Azure SQL database.
Review source

column1: Where does ADR keep the persistent version store (PVS) for an Azure SQL user database?
column2:
Inside the user database, not tempdb.
In-row and off-row versions consume space within the database's storage allocation.
Review source

column1: How does ADR change transaction log retention for long-running transactions?
column2:
It permits aggressive log truncation despite active long-running transactions.
Persistent versions reduce the log history needed for traditional rollback.
Review source

column1: Why can ADR add overhead to write-intensive workloads?
column2:
Row versions need additional data space and transaction logging.
In-row versions can increase page splits, and logged versions can increase log volume.
Review source

column1: Why keep transactions short even when ADR makes recovery faster?
column2:
Long-running transactions can delay version cleanup and increase PVS size.
High transaction-abort rates also put pressure on PVS cleanup.
Review source

column1: Which dynamic management view reports ADR persistent version store metrics?
column2:
sys.dm_tran_persistent_version_store_stats.
Its persistent_version_store_size_kb column reports off-row kilobytes only, not in-row versions.
Review source
